title: Moonshot ships Kimi K3 open weights — the largest open-weight model ever released
subtitle: The 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model landed on Hugging Face at 00:00 UTC on July 27 under a Modified MIT license, roughly 1.4 TB of weights that anyone with the hardware can now inspect, fine-tune, and self-host.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Moonshot AI published Kimi K3's full weights on Hugging Face at 00:00 UTC on July 27, delivering on a schedule the company set at the World AI Conference in Shanghai on July 16. K3 is a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 896 experts and 16 active per token — roughly 50 billion active parameters at inference — a 1-million-token context window, and native vision support. In MXFP4 four-bit precision the download is about 1.4 TB, versus roughly 5.6 TB at 16-bit. The license is Modified MIT, which permits commercial deployment. Moonshot has run K3 on its hosted API and the kimi.com consumer product since the July 16 unveil; the weights drop is the step that hands the model to anyone with the infrastructure to run it.

This is the largest open-weight model ever released, by a wide margin. The previous open-weight ceiling — Kimi K2 at 1 trillion parameters — held for less than seven months. K3 pushes the frontier tier into a size class that until now sat only behind closed APIs, and it does so with an architecture designed to be economical at inference: activating 16 of 896 experts per token means per-token compute resembles a mid-size model even though the parameter count does not. That is why 1.4 TB of storage is a real number for well-resourced enterprises — a handful of H200 nodes or a single next-generation Blackwell rack can hold it — rather than a hypothetical.

The strategic backdrop matters. Moonshot released K3 the same weekend Nvidia and SK Group inked a $500-billion memory and data-center partnership and Nvidia reportedly moved toward a $250-billion backstop for OpenAI's Ohio compute hub. The closed-frontier labs are locking in decade-scale supply. Moonshot is running the opposite play: give the model away, capture mindshare with developers and Chinese enterprises facing US API access risk, and force Western labs to argue against a free frontier-scale competitor. It is the same open-weight escalation that Meta's Llama family started in 2023, scaled up by roughly two orders of magnitude and repositioned as a China-origin geopolitical move.

For learners: when a frontier-scale model becomes downloadable, the useful question shifts from 'which model is smartest' to 'which model can you own the deployment of.' Self-hosting K3 buys you data control, latency control, and immunity to a vendor changing pricing or terms — but it costs you the operational overhead of running 1.4 TB of weights across expensive accelerators. If your work touches regulated data, an evaluation of K3 versus your current closed-API stack is now a real decision, not a thought experiment. Read the license terms carefully — Modified MIT is not standard MIT — and treat the first 30 days of community fine-tunes and safety probes as your best signal for what the model actually does under adversarial use.
